review.summary: This paper conducts an empirical partial-identification study on operational 50-member weather ensemble forecasts (ECMWF IFS and AIFS ENS across 28 initialization dates in summer 2026). For 12-site portfolios, it uses linear programming over the 4,096 binary states to compute sharp lower and upper bounds on the probability that at least k sites exceed a fixed temperature threshold under three nested summary releases: (1) marginal exceedance probabilities only, (2) marginals plus one scalar aggregate second binomial moment, and (3) marginals plus all pairwise co-exceedance probabilities. While most unselected queries are trivial floor/ceiling cases, within the pre-specified informative stratum (2,871 queries) the mean compatible probability interval widths are 0.5139 for marginals, 0.3146 with the aggregate second moment (capturing 43.4% of the narrowing), and 0.0547 with pairwise probabilities. Crucially, sensitivity analyses demonstrate that the apparent near-identification from pairwise moments is heavily driven by exact zeros and finite support in a 50-member ensemble (where a median of only 19 out of 4,096 binary states survive zero-cell pruning): subsampling to 10 or 25 members artificially shrinks widths further, whereas relaxing moments by even 0.005 under arbitrary weights widens the mean pair bound from 0.0514 to 0.1858.

score_reasons.correctness: The linear programming formulations, integer-weight checks, and rank diagnostics are mathematically sound, numerically verified to tight tolerances, and interpreted with exceptional care regarding denominators and finite-sample artifacts.
score_reasons.verifiability: Data sources, exact forecast dates, lead times, LP formulations, solver tolerances, resampling blocks, and missing-data envelopes are documented in exhaustive detail.
score_reasons.novelty: The count-tail LP under marginal and pairwise constraints is established in operations research and systemic financial risk (e.g., Giglio 2016; Padmanabhan & Natarajan 2021), making the contribution a solid empirical translation to weather ensembles rather than a new methodology.
score_reasons.generality: The exact atom-based LP scales exponentially (2^n), restricting the study to small 12-site portfolios, and the quantitative pairwise tightness depends strongly on the 50-member finite ensemble size.
score_reasons.usefulness: The audit usefully quantifies how much spatial count ambiguity a single aggregate second moment resolves (43.4%) and why finite-ensemble pairwise bounds look artificially tight, though pairwise binary tables are rarely a practical compression format compared to raw binary masks or count curves.
score_reasons.clarity: Mathematical definitions, figures, and tables are precise, but the text is overloaded with repetitive methodological disclaimers, bibliographic access notes, and thirteen exploratory appendices that impede readability.

research_question.question: For fixed 12-site portfolios in operational weather ensembles, how tightly do marginal exceedance probabilities, an aggregate second binomial moment, and pairwise co-exceedance probabilities bound the probability that at least k locations exceed a temperature threshold, and how often do those bounds certify a binary cost-loss decision?
research_question.predictable_reason: Nested tightening across moment releases, widenings under moment relaxation, and high certification away from decision boundaries are guaranteed by construction, whereas the specific empirical magnitudes in operational weather forecasts (such as the scalar second moment capturing 43.4% of marginal-to-pair narrowing and zero-cell pruning driving pair tightness) required empirical measurement.

main_issues.issue: Limited practical motivation for the pairwise summary format: as shown in Section 4.4, for a 50-member 12-site binary problem, transmitting all pairwise probabilities takes 468 bits while the full coherent binary mask takes only 600 bits (and answers all subset queries exactly), and the portfolio count distribution takes only 144 bits. Thus, a delivery interface that provides all 66 pairwise binary probabilities at a fixed threshold instead of the binary mask or count curve is somewhat artificial.

Exponential scaling of the full-atom LP: solving over all 2^n binary states works cleanly for n=12 (4,096 states) but does not scale to realistic regional grids with hundreds of locations where compression of large ensembles is most needed.

Overly defensive and cluttered presentation: nearly every paragraph contains repetitive disclaimers about what the study does not claim, bibliographic verification levels (e.g., stating whether a cited paper was checked at abstract or full-text level inside the main prose), and audit-log details that distract from the scientific narrative.

At cost-loss ratio c=0.1, the pre-specified informative stratum filter (q_k >= 0.1) overlaps with the decision boundary so that every query in the stratum has q_k >= c; although transparently diagnosed in Section 4.2, a symmetric threshold window not truncated by the stratum filter would be cleaner.
Several tables (Table 7 and Appendices A, D, H, and M) have long string labels in the Stratum or Explanation columns that collide with or overlap the adjacent numeric column N.

strengths: Exceptional methodological rigor and intellectual honesty, explicitly separating trivial floor/ceiling queries (where q_k=0 or 1 or <=2 sites are uncertain) from genuinely uncertain informative queries.

Insightful diagnosis of why pairwise bounds appear tight in 50-member ensembles, using subsampled member sizes (M=10, 25, 50), surviving-state counts, and continuous vs. integer lattice moment perturbations to expose finite-sample zero-cell pruning.

Valuable comparison between worst-case partial-identification bounds and simple point reconstructions (showing that marginal interval midpoints and historical forecast-rank templates achieve much lower error against the empirical ensemble than worst-case interval widths suggest).
Complete, self-contained reproducibility design with explicit verification of LP primal/dual residuals, missing-data envelopes, and unresolved integer-program bounds.

closest_prior_work.citation: Giglio, S. (2016). Credit default swap spreads and systemic financial risk. ESRB Working Paper Series No. 15.
closest_prior_work.difference: Applies the same Hailperin count-tail linear program with marginal and pairwise probabilities to bound the probability that at least r banks default from bond and CDS prices, whereas the reviewed paper applies the formulation to spatial temperature exceedances in operational weather ensembles and audits finite-ensemble support effects.

closest_prior_work.citation: Padmanabhan, D., & Natarajan, K. (2021). Tree bounds for sums of Bernoulli random variables: A linear optimization approach. INFORMS Journal on Optimization, 3(1), 23-45.
closest_prior_work.difference: Formulates the count-tail probability bound problem for sums of dependent Bernoulli random variables under univariate and bivariate marginals and develops polynomial-time LP formulations on tree graphs, whereas the reviewed paper solves the full 2^12 atom LP on complete pairwise tables and scalar second moments from weather forecasts.

closest_prior_work.citation: Ramachandra, A. K., & Natarajan, K. (2023). Tight probability bounds with pairwise independence. SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics, 37(2), 516-555.
closest_prior_work.difference: Reviews classical Hailperin LP and Boros-Prekopa binomial-moment bounds and derives analytical bounds under pairwise independence, whereas the reviewed paper evaluates empirically dependent weather ensemble moments and retains all individual marginals alongside the aggregate second binomial moment.

closest_prior_work.citation: Schefzik, R., Thorarinsdottir, T. L., & Gneiting, T. (2013). Uncertainty quantification in complex simulation models using ensemble copula coupling. Statistical Science, 28(4), 616-640.
closest_prior_work.difference: Restores spatial and multivariate dependence from marginal post-processed distributions using empirical ensemble rank templates (a point reconstruction), whereas the reviewed paper computes sharp partial-identification bounds over all joint binary distributions compatible with released moment summaries.

closest_prior_work.citation: Cooper, F., Nath, S., Weisheimer, A., & Palmer, T. (2026). Histogram compression of large ensemble forecasts. EGU General Assembly 2026, EGU26-15706.
closest_prior_work.difference: Proposes compressing 1,000-member rainfall ensembles into per-location marginal histograms by sacrificing spatial correlation, which motivates the reviewed paper's audit of how much joint spatial exceedance ambiguity remains when only marginal or low-order moment summaries are delivered.
